title: Notes of Ministry - 73 - December 1978

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 73 - December 1 (2441)/Notes of Ministry - 73 - Decemb - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: Reference was made in the reading to the value of the glad tidings which have reached us.

The need for each of us is to be kept in the appreciation of these glad tidings, which is to know this theme—the Son of God. I thought the Lord would help us and deepen our appreciation of the good news that has reached us about God’s Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

We must admit that we often look for a turn of the tide in the world, perhaps anticipating that we might find some good news or some turn in world affairs, something which might suggest improvement. I think we must accept from the Scriptures that while materially in God’s ways we may prove mercy, and do, at the same time there is moral decline and deterioration. So the good news from God stands out more in all its distinctiveness and glory. Naturally, of course, we look for improved conditions. Where men seek for better wages and improved conditions, we have a certain sympathy with them. When you read in the encyclopaedia that in the days of Mr. Darby children were working in the mines for fifteen hours a day and little boys were being forced to clean chimneys for nine, ten, or more hours a day, you can thank God for certain improved conditions for men; but morally, whatever the conditions of man, whether he is in difficulty, or whether his circumstances have improved, without any question he has proved himself to be a fallen creature.
God’s glad tidings reach us in these circumstances. The good news is centred in a Man who is raised from among the dead. Death rests on everything here. There is no question about that.

None of us could possibly dispute it. Whether a person is an atheist or an agnostic, or whether he belongs to one of the multitudinous groups of christendom, no one can deny that death rests on everything here.

Now the good news presents to us the Man who has broken the power of death. You have heard that many times, have you not? How many times have you heard that? God’s good news is about a Man who is marked out Son of God by resurrection of the dead. He actually raised dead people into life. He Himself was raised from among the dead by the glory of the Father. I wish that we could have our affections more centred upon the Person of Jesus, the Son of God.

I think one of the objects of the glad tidings is to detach us from things here in our affections and attach us to another Man in another world, so that our hope and affections are vitally centred upon a Man who is risen and glorified, and not on any earthly hope. That does not mean to say that you are unnatural, that you do not sorrow over the loss of loved ones; but we sorrow not as those that have no hope because we have a certain hope of the coming of the Lord who has broken the power of death. I think what has often been said is true—that if Jesus raised one person from among the dead, then He could raise millions. He is going to.

They are going to be raised and changed. I would like, dear brethren, that it might lay hold on us. I would like Mr. Taylor’s prayer to be answered, perhaps it will be with some of us, that not only should we lay hold of the truth, but that the truth should lay hold of us. That was one of his prayers,
and that is very much needed, I think, with all of us, that the truth might lay hold of us. There is a Man who has been raised from among the dead and He is seated at the right hand of God.

Do you believe that? Does everyone here believe that? One has often said (I would not apologise for repeating it) that when that lays hold of a man or a woman, it will revolutionise his life, or her life. Material things will have a lesser hold upon them and spiritual things a greater hold. I think the gospel is intended, as I have said, to detach us from things here and attach us to another Man in another world.

So the good news cannot break down. It cannot change into bad news. There is no political change here; there is no change in government. It has been said that power corrupts and absolute power corrupts absolutely. That is true, except in the case of one Man. God has placed in the hands of one Man all power in heaven and upon earth. So we need not fear; we can go forward in God’s testimony and in the simple path of His will day by day. So that while power corrupts man, there is one Man who is beyond any suggestion of corruption, and in that Man’s hands God has placed everything. I think this should affect us, dear brethren.

I read these passages just to make a few simple suggestions for your consideration. If one man of God said, ‘I am just throwing out a few suggestions for you to think about’, what can I say? I will just throw out three suggestions for you to think about.

In the first passage read we get a reference to being “to another”. And that Other is He “who has been raised up from among the dead”. I think what is in mind is that that Person should be before us as an object, not ourselves any longer. We are not governed by the law, but Christ should be before us as an object. “To another”—Another is before us; this is the objective to which the writer of the epistle refers. We go through a very anxious process, maybe, in reaching it, but Christ is the object. Now I would like the younger men and women here, and the boys and girls, to think about that. It is presented as being the intention that “ye also have been made dead to the law … to be to another, who has been raised up from among the dead”. That is what God has in His mind for you. So, as in the Psalms, you find that at the beginning of Romans 7 Paul tells you the end that is to be reached when you have gone through the process. When you find in yourself that just the very things you do not want to do, you do, and the very things that you want to do, you do not do. God is passing you through a process so that you should reach a point in your soul when Christ is everything to you.

So, as I say, the intention is set out first, but then the experiences necessary to reach it are in the rest of chapter 7. And the man who is writing says at the end of this process, “There is then now no condemnation to those in Christ Jesus”. “No condemnation”—how wonderful that is! We have often been reminded that it does not say that you are not condemned. It says that to those in Christ Jesus there is no condemnation. That is, the thing just does not exist for them, and never will, because of what Christ has done. The condemnation was in Him; He took it. So Paul says, “There is then now no condemnation to those in Christ Jesus”, that is, as I have apprehended it, an objective statement; but it is intended to affect us; that is to say, it is a statement of truth, and I have no doubt that it refers to every believer in the Lord Jesus.

Now whether every believer in the Lord Jesus has reached it is quite another question, but it is true that to those in Christ Jesus—that is how God regards those who have faith in Christ—such a thing as condemnation does not exist. What a wonderful thing to be reached in your soul!

The vital secret of deliverance is occupation with another Man, that is with Jesus, and Jesus raised from among the dead. How is it brought to pass? It says, “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set me free from the law of sin and of death”. The same Holy Spirit that is in that Man in heaven is in me. Now I would like you to think about that for a moment, and not pass it over lightly. He is in glorified conditions, that is, Jesus is in glorified conditions, and the same Holy Spirit that is in Him as Man in glorified conditions is in me. What an immense privilege! Do you value it? I think as that Man is my object, despite my weakness, and the Holy Spirit is active in me, I come into the enjoyment of liberty. You say, ‘I find I fail’. That is no doubt true! And then what do you do? Brood over it? Wish you were better?

Try to improve yourself? That is not God’s way. I think, if I fail, the Spirit immediately turns me to another Man in whom there is no failure, so that He occupies me in my exercises all the time, not with myself as a failure, but with another Man. If I fail, He turns me away to that Man, and my mind and soul in the process become absorbed with Him.

Now one man of God said, ‘I cannot give you this, because God intends you to go this way experimentally and learn it for yourself’. Again, I might show you the way. If I give you a map and say, ‘There is Glasgow’, that will not get you to Glasgow, will it? You will have to take the journey to get there. So the Lord Jesus will support you and help you in the depth of your exercises so that you might come into the enjoyment of deliverance and know what it is to walk according to the Spirit and not according to the flesh.

Now I would encourage our younger people to take this up with the Lord. It has often been said (I know I am repeating perhaps what is well known to some, but not to all) that it is more difficult to get people into Romans 7 than to get them out of it.. In these days when people are getting higher education I think there is less likelihood of their learning what they are in the flesh.

Then the same man of God also said that the reason people do not get peace is because they do not really believe they are as bad as God knows them to be. We need to look into these things, dear brethren, and then enter into them and get hold of them. So Paul says about sin in the flesh, “What the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God having sent his own Son, in likeness of flesh of sin, and for sin, has condemned sin in the flesh”. It will never be improved. What I am naturally and morally, as man of Adam’s order, will never be improved; God has condemned it entirely. There is presented to us another Man, that is Christ, and another power altogether, that is the Holy Spirit, and thus we are to be brought into liberty. If we are not brought into liberty, I doubt if we can rightly have our part in the service of God, because for that we must be set free.

The writer proceeds down the passage (I will not go into all the details) until he comes to the point where he says, “For ye have not received a spirit of bondage again for fear”, that is slavish fear, “but ye have received a spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father”. It is not crying, “Abba, Father”, because we think we ought to, but because we have received a spirit of adoption. Now I would like to ask each of us here if we have received the Spirit. Chapter 5 tells us that the Spirit has been given (Romans 5: 5); He sheds abroad the love of God in our hearts. There it is the Spirit given, but here, “Ye have not received a spirit of bondage again for fear, but ye have received a spirit of adoption (or sonship) whereby we cry, Abba, Father”. Now this is very vital, especially for you younger people. Only this morning we were speaking about a man who was brought up amongst the brethren and took an active, leading part; then he went right away and evidently comparatively recently said, ‘I have just been converted’; before that it was all head knowledge. Now that could be true of any one of us. So I would submit to the younger people especially that you take this matter up with the Lord Jesus, so that you might receive the Holy Spirit and understand that, as receiving the Holy Spirit, you have received a spirit of adoption, or sonship, that we might cry, “Abba, Father”. What a wonderful relationship we are brought into! Are we all crying, “Abba, Father”? We have our ups and downs in life—of course we do—maybe alternating moods of exuberance and depression; perhaps one day we are singing and the next sighing. And yet we “have received a spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father”. It is not simply in the meeting that we are crying, and, I believe, do cry, “Abba, Father”, but it is to characterise us.

Therefore I would like to exercise every one of us, and particularly those who are young, about the reception of the gift of the Holy Spirit. .If you have not received the gift of the Holy Spirit, whatever you may know, you are outside the life of christianity. You might know all its terms, you might know the glad tidings and even be able to preach it, but if you have not received the Holy Spirit you are outside the vitality of christianity. Now does this suggest that God is reluctant to give? In chapter 5 it says He has given us the Holy Spirit. The question is that as we received the Lord Jesus as Saviour have we received the Holy Spirit from Him as a glorified Man? Have I received Him? Have you received Him? I can say, thank God, I have received God’s Holy Spirit and He is an indissoluble bond between myself and the Man in heaven. Mind you, I wish I enjoyed it more! I acknowledge that; but, at any rate, I am conscious that I have received the Holy Spirit. Now, are you?

That is going to have an effect. It will have an effect in the mind, and if in the mind, in the whole being. So that the glad tidings intends that you should be secured in your whole spirit and soul and body for God, the whole of you for God! It does not alter your normal daily life.

It is often said that a person’s circumstances are not changed when he receives the gospel; it is the man or woman who is changed. What is in mind is that you should be secured, not partially, but wholly for God, so that God is before you in our Lord Jesus Christ.

So I read the passage in Romans 12 because Paul says there, “I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the compassions of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice”. “Your bodies”—now it has frequently been said that is the last thing that you want to give up.
Forgiveness of sins, well, that is very good—
‘My sins—O the bliss of this glorious thought—
My sins—not in part, but the whole—
Were borne on the cross, and are gone evermore.

Praise the Lord, praise the Lord, O my soul!’(Hymn 238) But when it comes to presenting my body a living sacrifice, I hesitate. Do you not? Reference was made earlier to a young man who admitted sadly that sometimes he had gone through the service of God quite unmoved. It was remarked that at any rate he was honest. We need to be honest, and I would be honest in saying that I have learned from experience that what another has said is true—that the last thing I will give up to the will of another is my body. Why is that? Because it is in my body that I indulge myself, it is in my body that I go where I please and do what I please. You do not go to a football match in your spirit—you might, of course, in a sense do that—but really you go to a football match, or you go to the pictures or the theatre, wherever it is you go, in your body. It is in our body that you and I enjoy doing our own will, and that is why my body is the last thing that I am prepared to give up, the last thing that I am prepared to present to God. Yet the apostle beseeches them to do it.

“And be not conformed to this world”—you can see how your body enters into that, can you not? Conformation to this world, following its practices, its pleasures, its dress, its fashions, whatever it may be. “Be not conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind”. Now the mind is the controlling faculty—it says, “be transformed by the renewing of your mind”, so that you are no longer pursuing your own will, but God’s will in your body. So Paul ends, “That ye may prove what is the good and acceptable and perfect will of God”. That is the will that Jesus did. He did it perfectly Himself—“Lo, I come to do, O God, thy will”, Hebrews 10: 7.

Now God is, through the glad tidings, securing a company of persons here who are like Jesus, doing His will in their bodies. You notice, “Present your bodies a living sacrifice”. While ‘bodies’ is in the plural, ‘sacrifice’ is in the singular. I think that is why he leads on to the truth as to the one body in Christ; but that is not quite the thought I am seeking to press, but rather the presenting of our bodies, the readiness to be secured by the glad tidings entirely for God in our whole spirit and soul and body. Think of what it cost Jesus in doing the will of God. It says, “By which will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all”, Hebrews 10: 10. It is because He did the will of God; that involved our sanctification. Where do you stand in the light of this? Where do I stand?

I think the Lord would speak to us encouragingly; He never speaks discouragingly, and if He raises the question with us as to whether we have received the Spirit, He is not condemning us because we have not, but encouraging us that we might. The Lord always speaks encouragingly, showing what is available in the glad tidings and what is available from Himself. I would urge that each of us, in exercise with the Lord, takes up these matters so that the glad tidings might have its effect, and as we are brought into the joy of it so we enter more livingly, with more spring, into the praise of God.

Now just a brief word as to the last passage which we read—“Let not then your good be evil spoken of; for the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. For he that in this serves the Christ is acceptable to God and approved of men”. “For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking”—men make an awful lot of eating and drinking, in the western world in particular. You find it enters into almost every social and political function. When they arrange a seminar or a meeting one of the first things on the programme is ‘10 a.m. coffee’.
Eating and drinking—how much they enter into our lives; how much they enter into the life of men generally.

Paul says the kingdom of God is not that. Of course he is referring to eating and drinking as between persons who may disagree on what should, or should not, be eaten, but at the same time he introduces the truth of the kingdom of God as being nothing to do with that. He says it “is not eating and drinking, but righteousness ...”—that is, doing what is right. Now if God has reckoned me to be righteous on the principle of faith, surely He would expect me to be practically righteous. “Righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” are the consequences that are seen in persons who are in the good of the kingdom. “Righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit”, how wonderful that is! Think of being brought to that!

As another has said, you are brought under the moral sway of God. May the Lord help us, all of us, to be brought more under the moral sway of God, to get an impression of the greatness of the Person who is the theme of the glad tidings, the Son of God, Him who was raised up from among the dead by the glory of the Father, and as we are affected by the greatness of His Person to be increasingly attracted by Him and secured by Him in our whole spirit and soul and body for the glory of His God and Father. May it be so for His name’s sake.

articles.title: COMMUNICATIONS OF LOVE CONTINUE
articles.author: C. Dolding
articles.meeting: Word at the burial of Miss W. Bridge

paragraphs.text: I am sure the Lord would answer the desire expressed in prayer that He might give us a touch of His present love. He would always do that, and in a very special way on such an occasion as this. It is like the Lord, is it not, to do so. We would look for this, and be encouraged by the way Paul speaks of being with Him. It was certainly Paul’s great desire to be with Christ, “having the desire for departure and being with Christ”. I suppose this should be true of all of us. It has been well said that individually we long to go to be with Christ and collectively we long for Him to come. This desire would be with us all.

“It is very much better”, Paul says. We often say that, and quote the scripture, and it is infinitely true. We thank the Lord for His loving consideration for our beloved sister in this, taking her into what is very much better. How merciful too, we may say, as we think of His love that took her and has given her the joy of being with Him. She has departed to be with Christ, which is “very much better”. Not ‘the best’; not yet. The best, I suppose, awaits our glorified bodies. Oh, that is the best! but meanwhile, dear brethren, how sweet it is that the Lord will grant to those He takes what is very much better. Our hearts rightly and soberly mourn; we would not be without these feelings—God-given feelings—but for her it is “very much better”. It seems as if Paul had the choice—a remarkable thing—but our sister has not had the choice. The Lord has taken her, and that is His matter.

The verses in 2 Corinthians 12 link on with Christ’s present love, and that He is occupied even now with those who are with Him, for Paul speaks of his body, and he does not know whether he was in it or out of it. He was unconscious of the body, for he was caught up into paradise—a wonderful experience and, I suppose, unique to the apostle. But nevertheless our sister and many others who are in the region of paradise are there with Christ. And moreover it seems to indicate in this passage that communications of love continue, because Paul says he heard things said. How wonderful that is! But there it is; things were said and heard. We might say it would be enough to be in His presence, and of course it is, but there seems to be something more meanwhile, even in a disembodied state, for the body has nothing to do with the matter. The spirit is with Christ, and Paul was unconscious of the body, and yet he heard “unspeakable things said”.

Well, it was just that impression, dear brethren, that communications of love continue even now. How sweet! It would lift our hearts and spirits in adoration to Him. He laid the basis for His own to be there with Him. Some have been with Him long, and some very briefly, but nevertheless Scripture seems to show that communications of love continue. How wonderful!
We may well adore Him, and thank and praise Him, and be lifted up now in the consciousness of His present love.

The way in which Paul addresses Timothy as “man of God” has often drawn my mind to this scripture. It seems to bring out so much for us in the kind of day which these two letters have in mind. We recognise the divine authority of the word in what this epistle to Timothy presents, but with that authority there is immense depth of appeal. You feel that the beloved writer is continually seeking to get right into Timothy’s soul, to secure that man in total committal to interests so glorious and so precious.

It must have struck Timothy that the one who was to him a father spiritually should say, “O man of God”. It would awaken Timothy to the place he had in Paul’s affectionate regard, and raise with Timothy a challenge as to the use of such a term concerning him; the challenge, in the skill of the beloved writer, the skill of the Spirit, was of course intended. The term is not used of very many. It is used of Moses; it is used of Elijah; it is used of Elisha, and in the last two cases particularly it seems to become prominent in relation to circumstances of widespread public breakdown. The man of God is one that can then be called upon to bring in the touch of God Himself in grace, but in power. Think of the remarkable exploits of Elisha particularly; for example, he brought a young lad to life. That was a mighty working of divine power in a day of widespread public brokenness. A man of God was equal to that. Paul’s concern as to Timothy was that he should be equal, as equipped, of God, for the circumstances which he faced in the testimony. You seem to discern, running right through both of these letters, the fatherly and affectionate touch of Paul; yet there is always the urgent touch that would brook no interference, no delay, no slackness, in pursuing the testimony to which such glory attaches.

Many of his injunctions to Timothy are very forceful, and yet the fatherly touch is there; it is to help Timothy, in the stimulation that divine love delights to give, to come forward in the full expression of what God had committed into his hand.

Now Timothy had been long with Paul. He knew him well. I doubt not he had heard him pray, had heard him speak of his concern for the saints in the various places where he knew them—and there were many such places—and he proved to be, as Philippians tells us, “like-minded” with Paul. Now that is the first point of vital import as to Timothy. He was like-minded with Paul. Paul writes at a time when he has to say, “I have no one like-minded …” (Philippians 2: 20), but then he calls attention to Timothy. Now I ask myself, am I like-minded with Paul? A very penetrating question—am I like-minded with Paul? Paul would be thinking of interests standing related to the Man in the glory who had appeared to him on the Damascus road. What a touch he had had from Christ up there in the glory in which He appeared to him! He was constantly moving under the precious impulse of that experience of his.

Are we getting impulses from Christ? It may not be in the outstanding circumstances in which Saul of Tarsus first had an impulse from Christ, but do we know what it is to get impressions from Jesus, directing us, guiding us, stimulating us, nourishing us, strengthening us for His interests? What are our relations with Christ? I believe that is a key question in the midst of the challenges of the present time—what our love for Christ is, where we are in our relations with Him. I have thought a lot of late of Mary (Luke 10: 39), who sat at the feet of Jesus “listening to his word”. Whatever He said, Mary would attend to it. Do we know that place? It is open to us.

There is no hindrance to our being, in the way suggested there, at the feet of Jesus. Do we know that place? It is a very, very precious place, a very, very fruitful place in which to be, to get communications definitely and in love from Jesus Himself.
Now all this would enter into the history of Paul as Timothy knew it. Therefore, what a touch of moral power enters into every injunction of Paul to Timothy. He was an apostle, certainly.

That must be guarded. That is according to God, that he had apostolic authority; but I ask you to see the weight of fatherly appeal that enters into these letters, which have such practical application, to this present time. Think of this wonderful time of reviving, of what God wrought around 1830! I speak of it quite practically because it was undoubtedly of God, and things that are of God we are free to speak of on such occasions. The truth was unfolded, and saints were recovered to it and established in it; conflicts came, and attacks of the enemy, thank God, were overcome; the testimony went on, and the Lord showed His hand to be in it.

This went on, but alas other things intruded, great griefs came in; matters came into view which were altogether distinct in character from that which God had begun with. We have had to face them and judge them. It is of God that we should face them, and judge them. I do not particularise; it is not for us on such an occasion to particularise, but things have come in which have challenged the course of what was of God in life among His beloved people.

What, therefore, shall we do? The Spirit helps us to get back to the pure spring of that wonderful work of God which, began about one-hundred-and-fifty years ago. The matter is such a challenging one that we could not do it without divine help, but the Spirit helps us to get through the matter to taste the pure springs, the choice, refreshing springs full of Christ, full of the glory of Christ, full of the greatness of the work of Christ, and full of the assembly as the great answer to the heart of Christ. These are stupendous and glorious matters which have been opened out in the Spirit’s power. Let us get back to them, dear brethren, and let us keep in them, and let us provide something in our own day, so different as it is, that would measure up in some sense to this word, “O man of God”.

Are we ready? Are we ready to go on with God in a dark day? Are we ready to be, in some sense, His resource in a dark day? Think of Elijah and Elisha and Moses! How God used them! They were always under His hand to be used. I believe there is something about this word, “O man of God” bringing great appeal to bear. Timothy would never claim such a title in any official sense or in any sense of claim. He knew his beloved spiritual father Paul too well to venture any such claim, but the word “O man of God” is to stir Timothy and stimulate him, to bring the urgency of the position to bear on him in a day of grave and increasing departure. The question is real, dear brethren, whether we shall stand for Christ in love for Him in the midst of a day of continually increasing departure’. Our love is being tested. Our loyalty to Christ is being tested. He loves to test it to bring out its true quality and its true value; there is to be something to answer to the man of God.

This is not without its feminine counterparts. We have women in the Old Testament singularly used in the defence of what is precious to God. Think of a woman like Abigail, and of others that would come to our minds, persons that just stood true to God, so that God could come in and exercise His power. The expression “man of God”, I understand, includes that; that there is in some sense a vessel of divine power that God can use in the furtherance of what is of Himself. How precious to be in God’s hand! It is not to make anything of us, but to make everything of Him and of Christ and of the Spirit.

So Paul warns us against the love of money. The Spirit warns us from time to time in such letters as these of outstanding perils, and this is one of them. I do not elaborate upon it, but it impresses me, as being in this passage, as one of great moment at the present time. He says, “But thou, O man of God, flee these things …”, flee them; do not tamper with them, do not investigate them; flee them, because they can do nothing but damage to what is so precious to Christ. “Flee these things”. It is not only the love of money, of course; he mentions several things, but he says, “But thou, O man of God, flee these things”. There are usually things arising in our pathways that we need to flee from, things that present themselves, perhaps very plausibly, not perhaps seemingly very important things, and yet as they gain our attention we see that God is not in them. “Flee these things”.

Beloved brethren, it is a time of decisiveness on our part in loyalty to Christ; not for putting off decisions, not for temporising and allowing things to continue perhaps in view of dealing with them later. No—it is a time for decisiveness, and for definiteness in loyalty and love for Christ to come into expression. “Flee these things, and pursue righteousness, piety, faith, love, endurance, meekness of spirit”. What lovely features these are, so consistent with what came out in Jesus; lovely features! We are to pursue them. That is the positive, energetic side, which the apostle never fails to bring forward. We are to pursue “righteousness, (first, as always in these letters) piety, faith, love, endurance, meekness of spirit”. Endurance tests us, but we are to pursue it. It will show the moral fibre of the person; it will show that he is, indeed, a man of God in some sense of the word.

Who of us would not in such times of growing heartlessness disclose our true colours in loyalty and allegiance to Himself? “Strive earnestly in the good conflict of faith”, earnestly—you see there is to be no half-measure; “earnestly”, he says. He puts in that word under the touch of the Spirit to bring Timothy up to the full standard; let us be found, dear brethren, measuring up in these days to the full standard. The full standard, of course, is Christ, but let us measure up in some sense to the standard as he suggests it a little later, “Christ Jesus who witnessed before Pontius Pilate the good confession”; the Model of everything in witness, as in everything else, is in Jesus; but we are to conform to the full standard, to rise to the height of what God has committed to His saints, to rise to the height of what God has brought about in recovering His saints to what is precious to Himself.

There is a great field of holy and fruitful activity before us here, leading to what the beloved apostle finishes with, that is, this glorious doxology, “to whom be honour and eternal might, Amen”. The greatness of God shines out. Lovely, is it not? When you go over the truth, the greatness of God shines out as you speak of these things, as you speak of His activities, as you speak of His saints. You see the glory of God shining out, producing an answer for Himself in life.

Truly it is a wonderful system of things, to which God has called us. May we each, from the youngest to the oldest, have a full part in it as having some sense of what is found in the “man of God”, for His name’s sake.
Blest Lord, dwell Thou through faith within our hearts,
That we the breadth and length, the depth and height,
May apprehend, for what that love imparts
That passes knowledge, fills us with delight.
Thus into all the fulness of our God
May we be filled, whose glorious might excels
More than our highest thought could e’er afford,
According to the power that in us dwells.
Now unto Thee, blest Father, would we bow
And render glory that is due to Thee,
In the assembly in Christ Jesus now,
And to the ages of eternity.
Aberdeen.

The intermediate state, then, is not glory (for that we must wait for the body. It is raised in glory …); but it is blessedness where no unholy evil is. It is being with Christ Himself, the source of joy ineffable … How a spirit enjoys Christ we cannot tell as to the manner of it, but there is no difficulty whatever. My spirit enjoys Christ now, in spite of the hindrance of the poor earthen vessel it is in, and though now we see Him not, yet rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory. It is not my body which enjoys Him now, but my soul spiritually, with the hindrance of the earthen vessel, and absent from Him, then without the hindrance of the earthen vessel, and present with Him.

paragraphs.speaker: J. N.
paragraphs.text: Darby on “The State of the Soul After Death”. Coll. Wrtgs. Vol. 31, pp.Whilst there is the great and glorious thought that we are to join the heavenly, the ransomed throng, as we say, and to enter into the actual fact of sonship … yet there is that which precedes that, namely what we may hope for in joining the Lord. He says to the thief, “Today shalt thou be with me in paradise”. That is something to think of. Paul said in 2 Corinthians 12 that he did not know whether he was in the body or out of it. But he was in paradise, and that was a truth that he would bring into his ministry. So that those who are ministering, even if old, have hope in what is immediate, in view of the Lord’s coming or of His taking them to be with Him at any time.
“To depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better”—better even than the very best thing here; and Paul had learned to say that, and has taught us to say it too.

Could you think of greater happiness than to be removed from the presence of every trace of the Adam-man or his influence, and to be introduced to a region where there is nothing to distract from Christ, and from all the qualities and characteristics of Christ which are to be the delight of God, and the delight and life of the saints eternally? That is the very “far better”
portion of those who are with Christ. They enjoy what they truly enjoyed on earth, but they enjoy it now with Him in a state where there are no distractions.

THE HONEYCOMB The many scriptural references to honey and the honeycomb make this a very instructive subject and it was good to learn more about it from some bee-keepers. One hive we saw had a removable back and, through glass, you could watch hundreds of bees in constant activity. There can be 80,000 bees in a hive, all working for the common good. They may fly two or three miles in their search for flowers and research has shown that, when they get back, they perform a kind of ‘dance’ which shows other bees the direction in which they have found a new source of food. They have wonderful ability to navigate accurately between the hive and the food gathering grounds. The mature bees do the gathering of nectar and pollen; the younger ones keep the cells clean, feed the larvae, and receive and store in the cells the food brought in by the foragers. Others build the cells of the honeycomb.

How many lessons we may learn in all this! Let us all be working for the common good, bringing in food as a result of individual labour. Then when the food is brought back, let us be like the bees who fill the cells with good things, building one another up, getting the truth into one another’s minds and affections, so that there is constant growth in intelligent affection for Christ. How pleasing to the Lord is such activity in the assembly—selfless working for the gain of all, and the production of a complete, finished structure, the honeycomb, filled with what He delights to appropriate. In Luke 23 He took it and ate before them. References in the Song of Solomon show what this means to Him—“Thy lips, my spouse, drop as the honeycomb; Honey and milk are under thy tongue” (Song of Songs 4: 11), and in Song of Songs 5: 1, “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey”.

Let us be diligent in the workings of love so that localities may be marked by this sweetness for Christ, the more precious to Him because of all that has entered into its production. He delights both in the honeycomb and in the activity of love which secures it for Him.
